name: The Holm Oak of Parque Bensaúde

location.address: Parque Bensaúde, Estrada da Luz, 1600 Lisboa

story:
Four trees in Parque Bensaúde carry a national protection order, and the one the neighbourhood is proudest of is not among them. That is the cork oak, reckoned the oldest in Lisbon, standing elsewhere in the same park. The official list runs differently: two holm oaks, a red-flowering gum and a field maple.

This is the heavier of the two oaks. Its companion, about 50 metres away, is a tree you can get your arms around. This one is not: 3.12 metres of trunk, 21 metres of height, and the low dense crown of small hard leaves that holm oaks keep through winter.

The ground was private for most of that time. It began as the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate on the road out to Luz, and later carried the name of the Bensaúde family who owned it. Only in recent decades has anyone been free to walk under this tree.

All four were classified together in 2004. The register recorded this oak at 100 years old when it was measured in 2017, which puts it near 110 now. That is a surveyor's estimate rather than a count of rings, and holm oaks grow slowly enough that it could be out by a decade in either direction.

name: The Second Holm Oak of Parque Bensaúde

location.address: Parque Bensaúde, Estrada da Luz, 1600 Lisboa

story:
Two holm oaks in Parque Bensaúde were classified on the same day and recorded at the same age. One measures 3.12 metres round the trunk. This one measures 1.72.

They stand about 50 metres apart in the same soil, which is a useful reminder that girth and age are only loosely related. Light, water and whatever the roots hit underground do most of the deciding. This is also the shorter of the pair at 17 metres, and it is the one you can actually put your arms around, which is the quickest way to know you have found the right tree.

Holm oak is the evergreen workhorse of the Iberian countryside, dark and dense, holding its small leathery leaves right through winter. There is no bare season here and no autumn colour, so the tree looks much the same in January as in July.

The park around it was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate later held by the Bensaúde family and opened to the public as a municipal park off the Estrada da Luz. Both oaks were classified in 2004, alongside a red-flowering gum and an unusually thick field maple a short walk west.

The register logged 100 years at its 2017 measurement, so roughly 110 today, on a surveyor's estimate rather than a dated planting.

name: The Red-Flowering Eucalyptus of Parque Bensaúde

location.address: Parque Bensaúde, Estrada da Luz, 1600 Lisboa

story:
This is the smallest of the four protected trees in Parque Bensaúde and the only one on the list for what it does rather than what it is. At 7 metres tall and 1.45 metres round it is beaten on every measurement by its neighbours. Then high summer arrives and the whole crown goes scarlet.

Corymbia ficifolia comes from a narrow strip of coast in southwest Western Australia, a natural range small enough to drive across in an afternoon, and it has been planted around the mild parts of the world for exactly this: dense clusters of red flowers held above the leaves, lasting weeks and dropping a carpet underneath.

No age is recorded for it anywhere. It was classified in 2004 for its flowers and for being uncommon in the city rather than for any claim to antiquity, and nobody has dated it since.

It stands about 40 metres west of the larger holm oak, close to the field maple, so the park's four classified trees make one loop of a few minutes. Parque Bensaúde was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas before the council opened it, which is how a private planting of an Australian ornamental ended up on a public list. Somebody wanted red flowers in their own garden, and a century later the garden became everybody's.

best_time.label: high summer, when the whole crown turns scarlet

name: The Field Maple of Parque Bensaúde

location.address: Parque Bensaúde, Estrada da Luz, 1600 Lisboa

story:
A field maple with a 3.5 metre waist is an oddity. This is the modest one of the European maples, a hedgerow and woodland-edge tree that usually tops out around 15 metres and rarely gets thick, and this one has a trunk wider than either of the classified holm oaks standing a few dozen metres east of it.

It reaches 13.5 metres at the western end of Parque Bensaúde, the fourth of the four trees the state singled out here in 2004. No age is recorded for it. Field maples are hard to date without cutting into them and this one has never been surveyed for age, so the honest answer is that it is old enough to have grown far beyond the usual size, and no more precise than that.

Look at the leaves to be sure you have the right tree. Field maple carries small five-lobed leaves with blunt rounded tips, quite unlike the sharp-pointed maples of parks and streets, and older twigs often develop corky ridges you can feel with a thumb. In autumn it turns clear yellow, briefly, before Lisbon's mild weather takes the leaves off.

The park was the Quinta de Santo António das Frechas, a 17th century estate, which explains how a northern European maple got here at all. Somebody planted it in a private garden and let it get on with it.

name: The Paperbark of Jardim Constantino

location.address: Jardim Constantino, Rua Passos Manuel, 1150 Lisboa

story:
Lisbon has one prickly paperbark, and this is it. The Portuguese record of Jardim Constantino calls the tree unique in the city, which is a strong claim for a garden of a quarter of a hectare to hold.

Melaleuca styphelioides is an Australian tree grown for its bark: white, spongy, laid down in papery layers you can press a thumb into, peeling in sheets around a trunk 1.58 metres round. The leaves are small, stiff and sharp-tipped, which is the prickly half of the name. At 18 metres with an 11 metre crown it is the tall thin one in this garden. The fig a few steps away is the wide one.

The garden opened in 1889 and takes its name from Constantino José Marques de Sampaio e Melo, a florist. It runs to a lake, a playground and a statue of Prometheus, and it sits in Arroios two streets off the metro, so this tree has spent its whole life in a city square rather than a park.

It was classified in 1996, half a century after its neighbour. The register recorded 107 years when it was measured in 2017, so roughly 115 now, which would put it in the ground around 1910, a generation after the garden itself.

name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Jardim Constantino

location.address: Jardim Constantino, Rua Passos Manuel, 1150 Lisboa

story:
A garden of a quarter of a hectare in Arroios holds a fig with a 26 metre crown, which accounts for most of the shade in the place. Jardim Constantino is small: a lake, a playground, a statue of Prometheus and two protected trees. This is the wide one.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the east coast of Australia and was planted across Lisbon in the late 19th and early 20th centuries for exactly this reason. It grows fast, throws a dense crown, and drops the buttressing roots that make a mature specimen look like it is holding the ground down. At 24 metres tall on a trunk 2.33 metres round, this one has done the job.

It has been protected since 1947, which is early. The paperbark standing a few metres away had to wait until 1996 for the same status. The register recorded 107 years when the tree was measured in 2017, so roughly 115 today.

Lisbon has better known Moreton Bay figs, at Príncipe Real and in the Estrela garden, both of them on their own city-centre stages with a crowd in front of them. This one has a neighbourhood square, a bench underneath and no queue.

name: The Belas-Sombras of Jardim António Feijó

location.address: Jardim Antonio Feijo, Largo do Intendente area, 1100 Lisboa

story:
The two fattest trunks in this garden are not really wood. Phytolacca dioica, the bela-sombra, is a giant herb rather than a tree, and the swollen base that makes it look ancient is soft, water-storing tissue you could dent with a thumbnail. It grows fast, it produces no timber worth the name, and it falls apart earlier than its bulk suggests.

There are two of them here, and they came out almost identical: 10.45 and 10.4 metres round, 17.6 and 16.4 metres tall. They stand about 30 metres apart, one at the southeast corner of the garden and one at the top of it, so the visit is both or neither.

The garden wraps around the Igreja de Nossa Senhora dos Anjos, inaugurated in 1911, and the pair went in at roughly the time the church was finished. They were classified in 1947, among the earliest protection orders in Lisbon, and reclassified in 2018.

The register recorded them at 105 years when they were measured in 2015, so roughly 115 now. With a bela-sombra that figure is softer than usual. The trunk does not lay down the tidy annual rings you could count in an oak, so any age for one is worked back from size and from whatever the planting records say.

name: The Bela-Sombra of Praça António Sardinha
story:
The roots of this one come out of the ground looking like more trunks. The parish council's own account of Praça António Sardinha describes a century-old bela-sombra whose roots resemble trunks converging into one, which is a fair description of what a big Phytolacca dioica does. The base spreads into buttresses and folds until it is hard to say where the tree stops and the ground starts.

At 10.9 metres round it is thicker than either of the pair 600 metres away in Jardim António Feijó. Its crown reaches nearly 21 metres across on a tree only 16.2 metres tall, so it is wider than it is high.

None of that is wood. The bela-sombra is a giant herb from the South American pampas, all soft water-holding tissue, which is why it swells so quickly and why a careless machine can damage it in a way an oak would shrug off.

It stands beside a primary school, and when the square was rebuilt in 2023 the works were laid out around it. It was classified in 2000. The register recorded 105 years at the 2015 measurement, so roughly 115 now, an estimate from size rather than a dated planting.

name: The Dragon Tree of Quinta Conde dos Arcos

location.address: Parque Urbano da Quinta Conde dos Arcos, Alameda D. Afonso Henriques area, Olivais, Lisboa

story:
This dragon tree is more than twice as wide as it is tall: 6.2 metres of height under a crown almost 14 metres across, on a trunk 4.75 metres round. Dracaena draco grows that way on purpose. It puts up a stem, flowers, then forks, over and over, until an old one looks like an umbrella made of umbrellas.

Nobody can date it properly. Dragon trees lay down no annual rings, so every age published for one is worked back from the branching or from records. The register recorded 200 years when it was measured in 2010, which makes it roughly 215 now, and that is about as precise as this species allows.

It grows in the Quinta Conde dos Arcos, a private estate the Lisbon council expropriated in 1940 and later opened as a nine-hectare park in Olivais. The old palace holds the municipal gardening school. The parish council names this dragon tree as the one tree of public interest among the 28 species growing there, and runs free guided walks on set dates through the year.

The sap runs red where the bark is cut, which is where the name comes from. Dragon's blood was shipped out of the Canaries and Madeira as a dye and a medicine for centuries before anyone thought to plant one of these in Lisbon.

name: The Plane Tree of Hospital Pulido Valente

location.address: Hospital Pulido Valente, Alameda das Linhas de Torres 117, 1769-001 Lisboa

story:
The national register puts this plane tree at 364 years old. If that is right, it was standing here before the hospital, before the road and before most of Lumiar.

Treat the number carefully. It comes from the classification file opened in 1945 and has been repeated since, including in the book Árvores da Cidade, which gives the same 364 years and near-identical height and crown figures. Two sources, one origin, and nobody has ever dated the wood. Add the years since that survey and the register's own figure would make it about 375 today.

What has actually been measured is impressive enough on its own: 5.85 metres round the trunk, 28 metres tall, and a crown 37 metres across, nine metres wider than the tree is high. It fills the forecourt of the Edifício D. Carlos at Hospital Pulido Valente, and the hospital holds its anniversary events underneath it.

This is not a park. It is a working public hospital, and the tree stands in the open forecourt where you can see it without going near a clinical area, so go as you would go into someone's front garden and stay out of the way.

The London plane is the tree Lisbon planted everywhere in the 19th century for shade. This one, if the file is right, was already old when that fashion started.

name: The Plane Tree of Travessa do Arco da Torre

location.address: Travessa do Arco da Torre, 1400 Lisboa (Belem, near Avenida da Torre de Belem)

story:
Two minutes from the queue at the Torre de Belém, on a back lane most visitors never turn into, stands a plane tree 29 metres tall. Travessa do Arco da Torre runs parallel to Avenida da Torre de Belém, near Largo da Princesa, and this is the tree that overtops the rooflines along it.

The trunk is 3.75 metres round and the crown spreads to nearly 27.5 metres, close to park dimensions for something growing out of a public street with no garden around it. Street planes are usually cut back hard for the wires and the windows. This one has been left to spread.

The register recorded 150 years when it was measured in 2010, so roughly 165 now, and the independent coverage of Lisbon's classified trees gives it about the same. It was classified in 2000.

That age puts its planting in the 1860s, when Belém was still being stitched into the city and long before the waterfront acquired its monuments, its museums and its crowds. Everything that now draws several million people a year arrived within sight of this tree, and it has watched the lot from one street back, over the roofs, with a couple of parked cars underneath it.

name: The Monterey Cypress of Parque do Caramão da Ajuda

location.address: Parque do Caramao da Ajuda, Belem, 1300 Lisboa

story:
Monterey cypress has one of the smallest natural ranges of any conifer: two headlands on the California coast near Monterey, a few kilometres of cliff, and nothing else in the wild. It also grows happily almost anywhere mild and coastal, which is how one ended up roughly 9,000 kilometres away with a 3.9 metre trunk in a park above Belém.

At 18.5 metres tall with a 17 metre crown, this is a heavy, wide, dark tree, the shape Monterey cypresses take once the wind has had a few decades at them: horizontal limbs, flattened top, foliage in dense sprays that smell of lemon when crushed.

It stands in the Parque do Caramão da Ajuda, which is a public park and not the Tapada da Ajuda next door. That distinction is worth getting right before setting out, because the two are neighbours and only one of them has this tree.

Beyond the state register, nobody appears to have written it up. The register classified it in 2000 and recorded 85 years when it was measured in 2015, which puts it around 95 now, and those are the only figures anyone has published. It is a solid enough record as far as it goes, and it is the whole of what is known about this cypress.
